name: Garlic / ginseng / aloe scalp remedies

lead: Garlic, ginseng and aloe vera are plant ingredients people apply to the scalp as home remedies, hoping to slow hair loss and improve scalp condition for fuller-looking hair.
Users usually describe a stimulating or soothing effect, with circulation and scalp health as the proposed route. The sources reviewed contain no hair-growth studies of these plants.

paras: People apply juices, gels or extracts, or use commercial products containing them, to the scalp as part of a regular routine.
Wikipedia reports burns from topical garlic and possible rash or allergy from aloe gel. Ginseng has listed side effects when taken orally.

angle.text: Garlic, ginseng and aloe vera are used as folk scalp remedies by people who want to slow hair loss or improve scalp condition. They are applied as raw preparations, gels or in commercial products, with improved circulation and scalp health as the proposed route to regrowth. No hair-growth trials were found for these uses.

lead: Garlic, ginseng and aloe vera are plant ingredients that people apply to the scalp, or take by mouth, as natural approaches to hair thickness and scalp health. The aim is fuller-looking hair or a calmer, healthier scalp: garlic is rubbed on or blended into oils and gels, ginseng extracts appear in hair-care products and supplements, and aloe gel is used as a soothing, conditioning scalp treatment and appears in commercial shampoos [1][2][3].

Research on these ingredients for hair is small. A 2007 double-blind trial in 40 people with localised alopecia areata found that adding garlic gel to betamethasone cream gave a good response in 19 of 20 participants versus a significantly lower rate with placebo gel, and the authors described it as a possible adjunct [4]. A 2009 Korean trial of Korean red ginseng taken orally for 24 weeks in androgenic alopecia reported increases in hair density and thickness, using a Folliscope for measurement [5].

Wikipedia's entries on the plants describe safety points relevant to topical use, notably burns reported from raw garlic applied to skin, including in children, possible rash or allergy from aloe gel, and side effects such as headache, raised blood pressure and insomnia for oral ginseng [1][2][3].
infobox: Garlic (Allium sativum), ginseng (Panax ginseng), aloe vera
Garlic gel in alopecia areata (2007); Korean red ginseng in androgenic alopecia (2009)

paras: Garlic has been applied to the skin in naturopathic practice and for acne. Wikipedia reports serious burns from such use, including in children, and discourages topical use of raw garlic [1].
For hair, the best-known study tested a 5 percent garlic gel combined with betamethasone valerate cream in alopecia areata, a patchy autoimmune hair loss, over three months [4].

Panax ginseng is a root used in East Asian folk medicine. Wikipedia lists headache, raised blood pressure, insomnia and rash as common side effects [2]. Reviews describe ginseng and similar plant adaptogens historically as extracts used to raise stability against physical loads [6].

A 2009 randomised trial in the Journal of Ginseng Research compared Korean red ginseng with placebo for 24 weeks in people with androgenic alopecia, measuring hair count, thickness and density with a Folliscope. The authors reported increased density and thickness in the ginseng group, with higher patient satisfaction and supportive photo ratings by dermatologists [5].

Aloe gel is used for minor burns and skin conditions, and cosmetic companies add aloe derivatives to shampoos, a use a review attributes to a moisturising, emollient effect. Wikipedia describes the evidence for wound and burn use as conflicting and notes possible burning, rash or allergic reactions [3].

Topical raw garlic has been linked to burns [1]. Garlic and some other herbal supplements have been associated with bleeding risk around surgery and interactions with anticoagulants [7][8]. Aloe gel can cause rash or allergic reactions [3]. Oral ginseng has listed side effects [2].

Garlic comes up on looksmax.org mostly in discussions of eating raw cloves for testosterone, where posters describe nausea and a burning mouth and one reply calls the idea a meme [9][10]. Scalp use is not a major theme in the threads reviewed.

Two small randomised trials have looked at hair outcomes. In the garlic study, 40 people with localised alopecia areata used garlic or placebo gel along with betamethasone for three months; 19 of 20 in the garlic group showed a good response versus fewer in the placebo group, with no complications observed [4]. In the ginseng study, Korean red ginseng taken by mouth for 24 weeks in androgenic alopecia increased hair density and thickness according to the authors [5].

No trial of aloe vera for hair growth was found. Other research on these plants covers blood pressure, cognition and fatigue rather than hair, such as reviews of garlic and hypertension [11] and ginseng and cognition [12].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, garlic is discussed mostly as a food said to raise testosterone; plant remedies for scalp hair appear less often [9][10].
